# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterized by delayed opacification of the epicardial coronary arteries in the absence of obstructive epithelial disease [1]. First systematically described by Tambe and colleagues in 1972, the condition was initially regarded as a curiosity but is now recognized as a clinically relevant cause of chest pain and recurrent hospital admission [2]. CSFP predominantly affects young to middle-aged men, often smokers, and contributes to a meaningful burden of myocardial ischemia and arrhythmic events [3].

## Definition and Diagnosis

CSFP is most reliably quantified using the corrected Thrombolysis In Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) frame count (TFC), introduced by Gibson et al., which provides an objective, reproducible measure of coronary flow [4]. A TFC exceeding two standard deviations above the established normal mean defines slow flow [5]. The condition must be distinguished from coronary no-reflow seen after percutaneous coronary intervention and from slow flow secondary to ectasia, spasm, or microembolization [6]. Importantly, CSFP is a diagnosis applied to angiographically near-normal vessels, separating it from obstructive coronary artery disease [7].

## Pathophysiology

The mechanisms underlying CSFP remain incompletely understood, but converging evidence implicates microvascular dysfunction as a central feature [8]. Histopathological studies of patients with CSFP have demonstrated fibromuscular hyperplasia, myointimal proliferation, and endothelial degeneration within small coronary vessels [9]. Endothelial dysfunction, reflected by reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and impaired flow-mediated dilation, is consistently reported [10]. Elevated markers of systemic inflammation, including C-reactive protein, interleukin-6, and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, suggest a contributory inflammatory state [11]. Oxidative stress, with increased markers of lipid peroxidation and reduced antioxidant capacity, has likewise been observed [12]. Some investigators have proposed diffuse atherosclerosis below the threshold of angiographic visibility, supported by intravascular ultrasound findings of intimal thickening and calcification [13]. Abnormalities in platelet function and a prothrombotic milieu have also been described [14].

## Clinical Features

The dominant clinical presentation is recurrent chest pain, frequently occurring at rest and sometimes mimicking acute coronary syndrome [15]. A substantial proportion of patients present with unstable angina, and troponin elevation can occur [16]. CSFP has been associated with electrocardiographic abnormalities including prolonged QT interval, increased QT dispersion, and fragmented QRS, all of which raise concern for arrhythmic susceptibility [17]. Indeed, life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death, while uncommon, have been reported [18]. Impaired left ventricular diastolic function and subtle systolic abnormalities detectable by strain imaging are also documented [19]. The condition recurs and is a frequent cause of repeated emergency department visits, contributing to impaired quality of life [20].

## Associated Conditions and Risk Factors

CSFP is linked to several metabolic and cardiovascular risk factors. Cigarette smoking, male sex, and elevated body mass index are recurrent associations [21]. Metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, and abnormal glucose handling appear overrepresented [22]. Dyslipidemia, particularly elevated low-density lipoprotein and reduced high-density lipoprotein, has been reported [23]. An association with obstructive sleep apnea and with elevated homocysteine has also been suggested [24].

## Management

There is no universally accepted treatment for CSFP, and management is largely empirical and aimed at symptom relief [25]. Dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, particularly mibefradil and diltiazem, have improved TFC and reduced angina in small trials [26]. Dipyridamole and nicorandil, agents acting on the microvasculature, have shown benefit in improving coronary flow [27]. Statins, through pleiotropic anti-inflammatory and endothelial-stabilizing effects, may improve flow and symptoms [28]. Nebivolol, a beta-blocker with nitric-oxide-mediated vasodilatory properties, has demonstrated favorable effects on coronary microvascular function [29]. Aggressive risk-factor modification, including smoking cessation and management of dyslipidemia and glucose intolerance, remains a cornerstone of care [30].

## Conclusion

CSFP is an increasingly recognized clinical entity that lies at the intersection of microvascular dysfunction, endothelial impairment, and systemic inflammation. Although generally considered benign, its association with refractory angina, arrhythmia, and rare sudden death warrants attention. Standardized diagnostic criteria using the corrected TIMI frame count have improved recognition, yet robust randomized trials of therapy are lacking. Future research should clarify the underlying pathophysiology and establish evidence-based treatment strategies to relieve symptoms and improve outcomes.
